title: SA road deaths mount as severity outpaces crash frequency
full_text:
South Australia’s road fatality count reached 60 in the first half of 2026 – already 69% of the state’s entire 2025 annual toll – placing the competitive compulsory third-party insurance scheme under its most significant claims-environment test since private underwriting began a decade ago. The figures, published July 14 by the Royal Automobile Association of South Australia (RAA), represent a 58% year-on-year rise from the 38 deaths recorded in the same period of 2025. The toll sits 30% above the state’s five-year average, with 444 people suffering serious injuries over the same six months.
For the five insurers writing CTP in the state, the pattern embedded in the SA Police collision data is particularly instructive: total casualties year-to-date to mid-July 2026 rose just 0.76% on the same point in 2025, while fatalities rose 47.62% and serious injuries rose 4.25% over the same comparison. Crash volume has remained broadly stable – it is the severity of outcomes that has deteriorated, a profile that carries distinct actuarial implications for long-tail bodily injury reserving.
The deterioration extends a trajectory that was already off course. South Australia’s Road Safety Strategy to 2031 requires the state to record fewer than 43 deaths and 474 serious injuries per year by 2031. By the end of the first quarter of 2026 alone, 32 fatalities and 226 serious injuries had already been recorded. Full-year 2024 data showed 89 lives lost and 809 people seriously injured on South Australian roads – more than double and well above those annual targets, respectively.
RAA senior traffic engineer Matt Vertudaches said the pace of decline was not in doubt. “A mid-year total 30% higher than average puts us on a devastating trajectory and shows we cannot become complacent about road safety. We’re only halfway through the year and well behind where South Australia needs to be to meet the targets set out in the State Road Safety Strategy to 2031,” Vertudaches said.
South Australia Police raised a similar alarm in May, when the toll had reached 44 – a four-year high at that point. SAPOL traffic services branch officer in charge, superintendent Shane Johnson, said the figures were deeply concerning. “Any fatality on our roads is a serious tragedy. The number of deaths and serious accidents we have had this year is significantly higher than SAPOL’s target, and I urge South Australian road users to be more careful,” Johnson said, as reported by Mirage News.
South Australia’s CTP insurance is provided by five government-approved insurers – AAMI, Allianz, NRMA, QBE, and Youi – under a competitive, privately underwritten scheme established in 2016 and overseen by the independent CTP Insurance Regulator. The scheme operates on a community rating model, meaning all owners of a particular vehicle class pay the same premium based on the claims experience of that class, regardless of individual driver history. A sustained increase in crash severity – rather than frequency – feeds into scheme costs through larger individual claims, longer recovery periods, and higher per-claim liability exposures.
The CTP Insurance Regulator’s 2024-25 annual report noted that the majority of South Australian motorists saw premium increases below inflation for 2025-26, with the lowest available metropolitan private passenger vehicle premium representing 14% of South Australian average weekly earnings – down from 27% when the scheme commenced in 2016. Those settings predated the first-half 2026 data. The regulator is required to set premium bands at least annually using independent actuarial analysis. A precedent for mid-year intervention exists: the 2023-24 annual report recorded the regulator’s first-ever mid-year premium review, which resulted in changes to premium bands.
The SA Police data also reveals significant year-on-year increases among specific road user groups that carry distinct CTP implications. Motorcycle rider fatalities stood at 13 year-to-date to mid-July 2026, up 160% on the five recorded at the same point in 2025. Pedal cyclist deaths reached six, up from one in the same period last year. P-plate driver fatalities reached eight year-to-date, up 166.67% on three at the same point in 2025.
Among serious injuries, e-scooter rider injuries have increased 300% year-to-date compared with the same period in 2025, from three to 12. South Australia legalised privately owned e-scooters and other personal mobility devices on public roads from July 13, 2025. The data captures the first full comparable period since legalisation – and suggests a claims exposure that was not present at all in the prior scheme year.
RAA senior traffic engineer Vertudaches said vulnerable road users were becoming a growing proportion of total road trauma. “While vehicle occupant fatalities have declined over past decades, our most vulnerable road users are becoming increasingly represented in road trauma. Too many crashes continue to involve behaviours we know are preventable, including speeding, distraction, dangerous behaviour, impairment, and failing to wear a seatbelt,” he said.
Regional roads accounted for 63% of all fatalities in the first half of 2026. The SA Police data shows the Hills Fleurieu region recorded serious injuries up 28.3% year-to-date versus the same period in 2025, and the Yorke Mid North region was up 21.05%. BITRE’s Road Trauma Australia 2024 report found per capita death rates in inner and outer regional areas are four to five times higher than in major cities, a disparity that compounds scheme liability given longer hospital transfer times and higher injury severity in regional crashes.
BITRE found the national per capita road death rate increased at an average of 3% per year since a low in 2020, reaching 4.78 deaths per 100,000 population in 2024. For the 12 months to May 2026, New South Wales recorded 365 deaths (up 8.6%) and Queensland recorded 330 (up 10.4%), per BITRE’s monthly bulletin. The national trend confirms rising road trauma is a systemic pressure on CTP schemes across Australia – though South Australia’s per capita position, its community-rated scheme structure, and the severity-driven nature of its 2026 deterioration make its exposure more acute than aggregate national figures suggest.
